# camino - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camino/

## Expand description

UTF-8 encoded paths.

`camino` is an extension of the [ std::path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/index.html) module that adds new

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html)

`Utf8PathBuf`[types. These are like the standard library’s](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)

`PathBuf`[types, except they are guaranteed to only contain UTF-8 encoded data. Therefore, they expose the ability to get their contents as strings, they implement](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[, etc.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Display.html)

`Display`The [ std::path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/index.html) types are not guaranteed to be valid UTF-8. This is the right decision for the standard library,
since it must be as general as possible. However, on all platforms, non-Unicode paths are vanishingly uncommon for a
number of reasons:

- Unicode won. There are still some legacy codebases that store paths in encodings like Shift-JIS, but most have been converted to Unicode at this point.
- Unicode is the common subset of supported paths across Windows and Unix platforms. (On Windows, Rust stores paths
as [an extension to UTF-8](https://simonsapin.github.io/wtf-8/), and converts them to UTF-16 at Win32 API boundaries.)
- There are already many systems, such as Cargo, that only support UTF-8 paths. If your own tool interacts with any such system, you can assume that paths are valid UTF-8 without creating any additional burdens on consumers.
- The [“makefile problem”](https://www.mercurial-scm.org/wiki/EncodingStrategy#The_.22makefile_problem.22)(which also applies to`Cargo.toml`, and any other metadata file that lists the names of other files) has*no general, cross-platform solution*in systems that support non-UTF-8 paths. However, restricting paths to UTF-8 eliminates this problem.

Therefore, many programs that want to manipulate paths *do* assume they contain UTF-8 data, and convert them to [ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)s
as  necessary. However, because this invariant is not encoded in the

[type, conversions such as](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path``path.to_str().unwrap()` need to be repeated again and again, creating a frustrating experience.Instead, `camino` allows you to check that your paths are UTF-8 *once*, and then manipulate them
as valid UTF-8 from there on, avoiding repeated lossy and confusing conversions.

# camino 1.2.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/camino/latest

# camino - UTF-8 paths

This repository contains the source code for `camino`, an extension of the `std::path` module that adds new
[ Utf8PathBuf](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html) and

[types.](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`## What is camino?

`camino`'s [ Utf8PathBuf](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html) and

[types are like the standard library's](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)

`PathBuf`[types, except they are guaranteed to only contain UTF-8 encoded data. Therefore, they expose the ability to get their contents as strings, they implement](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path``Display`, etc.The `std::path` types are not guaranteed to be valid UTF-8. This is the right decision for the standard library,
since it must be as general as possible. However, on all platforms, non-Unicode paths are vanishingly uncommon for a
number of reasons:

- Unicode is now the dominant encoding for file names. There are still some legacy codebases that store paths in encodings like [Shift JIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shift_JIS), but most have been converted to Unicode at this point.
- Unicode is the common subset of supported paths across Windows and Unix platforms. (On Windows, Rust stores paths
as [an extension to UTF-8](https://simonsapin.github.io/wtf-8/), and converts them to UTF-16 at Win32 API boundaries.)
- There are already many systems, such as Cargo, that only support UTF-8 paths. If your own tool interacts with any such system, you can assume that paths are valid UTF-8 without creating any additional burdens on consumers.
- The ["makefile problem"](https://www.mercurial-scm.org/wiki/EncodingStrategy#The_.22makefile_problem.22)asks: given a Makefile or other metadata file (such as`Cargo.toml`) that lists the names of other files, how should the names in the Makefile be matched with the ones on disk? This has*no general, cross-platform solution*in systems that support non-UTF-8 paths. However, restricting paths to UTF-8 eliminates this problem.

Therefore, many programs that want to manipulate paths *do* assume they contain UTF-8 data, and convert them to `str`s
as necessary. However, because this invariant is not encoded in the `Path` type, conversions such as
`path.to_str().unwrap()` need to be repeated again and again, creating a frustrating experience.

Instead, `camino` allows you to check that your paths are UTF-8 *once*, and then manipulate them
as valid UTF-8 from there on, avoiding repeated lossy and confusing conversions.

## Examples

The documentation for [ Utf8PathBuf](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html) and

[contains several examples.](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`For examples of how to use `camino` with other libraries like `serde` and `clap`, see the [ camino-examples](https://github.com/camino-rs/camino/tree/main/camino-examples) directory.

## API design

`camino` is a very thin wrapper around `std::path`. [ Utf8Path](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html) and

[are drop-in replacements for](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html)

`Utf8PathBuf`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)

`PathBuf`Most APIs are the same, but those at the boundary with `str` are different. Some examples:

- `Path::to_str() -> Option<&str>`has been renamed to- `Utf8Path::as_str() -> &str`.
- `Utf8Path`- `Display`, and- `Path::display()`has been removed.
- Iterating over a `Utf8Path``&str`, not`&OsStr`.

Every [ Utf8Path](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html) is a valid

[, so](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[implements](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path``AsRef<Path>`. Any APIs that accept `impl AsRef<Path>`
will continue to work with [instances.](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`## Should you use camino?

`camino` trades off some utility for a great deal of simplicity. Whether `camino` is appropriate for a project or not
is ultimately a case-by-case decision. Here are some general guidelines that may help.

*You should consider using camino if...*

- **You're building portable, cross-platform software.**While both Unix and Windows platforms support different kinds of non-Unicode paths, Unicode is the common subset that's supported across them.
- **Your system has files that contain the names of other files.**If you don't use UTF-8 paths, you will run into the makefile problem described above, which has no general, cross-platform solution.
- **You're interacting with existing systems that already assume UTF-8 paths.**In that case you won't be adding any new burdens on downstream consumers.
- **You're building something brand new and are willing to ask your users to rename their paths if necessary.**Projects that don't have to worry about legacy compatibility have more flexibility in choosing what paths they support.

In general, using camino is the right choice for most projects.

*You should  NOT use camino, if...*

- **You're writing a core system utility.**If you're writing, say, an- `mv`or- `cat`replacement, you should- **not**use camino. Instead, use- `std::path::Path`
- **You have legacy compatibility constraints.**For example, Git supports non-UTF-8 paths. If your tool needs to handle arbitrary Git repositories, it should use its own path type that's a wrapper around- `Vec<u8>`.- `std::path::Path`- [on Unix](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/ffi/index.html)but not on Windows.

- **There's some other reason you need to support non-UTF-8 paths.**Some tools like disk recovery utilities need to handle potentially corrupt filenames: only being able to handle UTF-8 paths would greatly diminish their utility.

## Optional features

By default, `camino` has **no dependencies** other than `std`. There are some optional features that enable
dependencies:

- `serde1`adds serde- `Serialize`- `Deserialize`- `Utf8PathBuf`- `Utf8Path`
- `proptest1`adds- [proptest](https://altsysrq.github.io/proptest-book/)- `Arbitrary`- `Utf8PathBuf`- `Box<Utf8Path>`.

## Rust version support

The minimum supported Rust version (MSRV) for `camino` with default features is **1.61**. This project is tested in CI
against the latest stable version of Rust and the MSRV.

- *Stable APIs*added in later Rust versions are supported either through conditional compilation in- `build.rs`, or through backfills that also work on older versions.
- *Deprecations*are kept in sync with the version of Rust they're added in.
- *Unstable APIs*are currently not supported. Please- [file an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/camino-rs/camino/issues/new)if you need an unstable API.

`camino` is designed to be a core library and has a conservative MSRV policy. MSRV increases will only happen for
a compelling enough reason, and will involve at least a minor version bump.

Optional features may pull in dependencies that require a newer version of Rust.

license](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT).

or the [MIT license](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/LICENSE-MIT).

# proptest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proptest/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#proptest-reference-documentation)Proptest Reference Documentation

This is the reference documentation for the proptest API.

For documentation on how to get started with proptest and general usage
advice, please refer to the [Proptest Book](https://proptest-rs.github.io/proptest/intro.html).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/index.html)
- Defines the `Arbitrary`trait and related free functions and type aliases.
- [array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html)
- Support for strategies producing fixed-length arrays.
- [bits](https://docs.rs/bits/index.html)
- Strategies for working with bit sets.
- [bool](https://docs.rs/bool/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `bool`values.
- [char](https://docs.rs/char/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `char`values.
- [collection](https://docs.rs/collection/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `std::collections`of values.
- [num](https://docs.rs/num/index.html)
- Strategies to generate numeric values (as opposed to integers used as bit fields).
- [option](https://docs.rs/option/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `std::Option`values.
- [path](https://docs.rs/path/index.html)- `std`
- Strategies for generating [`PathBuf`] and related path types.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Re-exports the most commonly-needed APIs of proptest.
- [range_](https://docs.rs/range_subset/index.html)- subset - `std`
- Strategies for generating values by taking samples of index ranges.
- [result](https://docs.rs/result/index.html)
- Strategies for combining delegate strategies into `std::Result`s.
- [sample](https://docs.rs/sample/index.html)
- Strategies for generating values by taking samples of collections.
- [strategy](https://docs.rs/strategy/index.html)
- Defines the core traits used by Proptest.
- [string](https://docs.rs/string/index.html)- `std`
- Strategies for generating strings and byte strings from regular expressions.
- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_runner/index.html)- runner
- State and functions for running proptest tests.
- [tuple](https://docs.rs/tuple/index.html)
- Support for combining strategies into tuples.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert.html)- assert
- Similar to `assert!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert_eq.html)- assert_ - eq
- Similar to `assert_eq!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert_ne.html)- assert_ - ne
- Similar to `assert_ne!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assume.html)- assume
- Rejects the test input if assumptions are not met.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_compose.html)- compose
- Convenience to define functions which produce new strategies.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_oneof.html)- oneof
- Produce a strategy which picks one of the listed choices.
- [proptest](https://docs.rs/macro.proptest.html)
- Easily define `proptest`tests.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [property_](https://docs.rs/attr.property_test.html)- test - `attr-macro`
- The `property_test`procedural macro simplifies the creation of property-based tests using the`proptest`crate. This macro provides a more concise syntax for writing tests that automatically generate test cases based on properties.

# serde_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/^1/

## Expand description

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The `serde_core` crate contains Serde’s trait definitions with **no support
for #[derive()]**.

In crates that derive an implementation of `Serialize` or `Deserialize`, you
must depend on the [ serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde) crate, not

`serde_core`.In crates that handwrite implementations of Serde traits, or only use them
as trait bounds, depending on `serde_core` is permitted. But `serde`
re-exports all of these traits and can be used for this use case too. If in
doubt, disregard `serde_core` and always use `serde`.

Crates that depend on `serde_core` instead of `serde` are able to compile in
parallel with `serde_derive` even when `serde`’s “derive” feature is turned on,
as shown in the following build timings.

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde` |

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde_core` |

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

# bincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bincode/^1/

## Expand description

Bincode is a crate for encoding and decoding using a tiny binary serialization strategy. Using it, you can easily go from having an object in memory, quickly serialize it to bytes, and then deserialize it back just as fast!

[§](https://docs.rs#using-basic-functions)Using Basic Functions

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    // The object that we will serialize.
    let target: Option<String>  = Some("hello world".to_string());
    let encoded: Vec<u8> = bincode::serialize(&target).unwrap();
    let decoded: Option<String> = bincode::deserialize(&encoded[..]).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(target, decoded);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#128bit-numbers)128bit numbers

Support for `i128` and `u128` is automatically enabled on Rust toolchains
greater than or equal to `1.26.0` and disabled for targets which do not support it

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.223/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# serde_bytes - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_bytes/^0.11.8/

## Expand description

Wrapper types to enable optimized handling of `&[u8]` and `Vec<u8>`.

Without specialization, Rust forces Serde to treat `&[u8]` just like any
other slice and `Vec<u8>` just like any other vector. In reality this
particular slice and vector can often be serialized and deserialized in a
more efficient, compact representation in many formats.

When working with such a format, you can opt into specialized handling of
`&[u8]` by wrapping it in `serde_bytes::Bytes` and `Vec<u8>` by wrapping it
in `serde_bytes::ByteBuf`.

Additionally this crate supports the Serde `with` attribute to enable
efficient handling of `&[u8]` and `Vec<u8>` in structs without needing a
wrapper type.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Efficient<'a> {
    #[serde(with = "serde_bytes")]
    bytes: &'a [u8],
    #[serde(with = "serde_bytes")]
    byte_buf: Vec<u8>,
    #[serde(with = "serde_bytes")]
    byte_array: [u8; 314],
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Byte](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteArray.html)- Array
- Wrapper around `[u8; N]`to serialize and deserialize efficiently.
- [ByteBuf](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteBuf.html)
- Wrapper around `Vec<u8>`to serialize and deserialize efficiently.
- [Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html)
- Wrapper around `[u8]`to serialize and deserialize efficiently.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- Types that can be deserialized via `#[serde(with = "serde_bytes")]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- Types that can be serialized via `#[serde(with = "serde_bytes")]`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [deserialize](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize.html)
- Serde `deserialize_with`function to deserialize bytes efficiently.
- [serialize](https://docs.rs/fn.serialize.html)
- Serde `serialize_with`function to serialize bytes efficiently.

# camino - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/camino/latest/target-redirect/camino/

## Expand description

UTF-8 encoded paths.

`camino` is an extension of the [ std::path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/index.html) module that adds new

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html)

`Utf8PathBuf`[types. These are like the standard library’s](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)

`PathBuf`[types, except they are guaranteed to only contain UTF-8 encoded data. Therefore, they expose the ability to get their contents as strings, they implement](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[, etc.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Display.html)

`Display`The [ std::path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/index.html) types are not guaranteed to be valid UTF-8. This is the right decision for the standard library,
since it must be as general as possible. However, on all platforms, non-Unicode paths are vanishingly uncommon for a
number of reasons:

- Unicode won. There are still some legacy codebases that store paths in encodings like Shift-JIS, but most have been converted to Unicode at this point.
- Unicode is the common subset of supported paths across Windows and Unix platforms. (On Windows, Rust stores paths
as [an extension to UTF-8](https://simonsapin.github.io/wtf-8/), and converts them to UTF-16 at Win32 API boundaries.)
- There are already many systems, such as Cargo, that only support UTF-8 paths. If your own tool interacts with any such system, you can assume that paths are valid UTF-8 without creating any additional burdens on consumers.
- The [“makefile problem”](https://www.mercurial-scm.org/wiki/EncodingStrategy#The_.22makefile_problem.22)(which also applies to`Cargo.toml`, and any other metadata file that lists the names of other files) has*no general, cross-platform solution*in systems that support non-UTF-8 paths. However, restricting paths to UTF-8 eliminates this problem.

Therefore, many programs that want to manipulate paths *do* assume they contain UTF-8 data, and convert them to [ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)s
as  necessary. However, because this invariant is not encoded in the

[type, conversions such as](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path``path.to_str().unwrap()` need to be repeated again and again, creating a frustrating experience.Instead, `camino` allows you to check that your paths are UTF-8 *once*, and then manipulate them
as valid UTF-8 from there on, avoiding repeated lossy and confusing conversions.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |

| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# sequoia_openpgp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sequoia-openpgp/2.4.0/sequoia_openpgp/

## Expand description

OpenPGP data types and associated machinery.

This crate aims to provide a complete implementation of OpenPGP as
defined by [RFC 9580](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html) as well as the deprecated OpenPGP as defined
by [RFC 4880](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc4880).  OpenPGP is a standard by the IETF.  It was derived
from the PGP software, which was created by Phil Zimmermann in
1991.

This crate also includes support for unbuffered message processing.

A few features that the OpenPGP community considers to be deprecated (e.g., version 3 compatibility) have been left out. We have also updated some OpenPGP defaults to avoid foot guns (e.g., we selected modern algorithm defaults). If some functionality is missing, please file a bug report.

A non-goal of this crate is support for any sort of high-level,
bolted-on functionality.  For instance, [RFC 9580](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html) does not define
trust models, such as the web of trust, direct trust, or TOFU.
Neither does this crate.  [RFC 9580](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html) does provide some mechanisms
for creating trust models (specifically, UserID certifications),
and this crate does expose those mechanisms.

We also try hard to avoid dictating how OpenPGP should be used. This doesn’t mean that we don’t have opinions about how OpenPGP should be used in a number of common scenarios (for instance, message validation). But, in this crate, we refrain from expressing those opinions; we will expose an opinionated, high-level interface in the future. In order to figure out the most appropriate high-level interfaces, we look at existing users. If you are using Sequoia, please get in contact so that we can learn from your use cases, discuss your opinions, and develop a high-level interface based on these experiences in the future.

Despite —or maybe because of— its unopinionated nature we found it easy to develop opinionated OpenPGP software based on Sequoia.

[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-features)Experimental Features

This crate may implement extensions where the standardization effort is still ongoing. These experimental features are marked as such in the documentation. We invite you to experiment with them, but please do expect the semantics and possibly even the wire format to evolve.

- Cryptographic primitives.

# tatara_hvf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-hvf/0.2.122/tatara_hvf/

## Expand description

`tatara-hvf` — Apple Hypervisor.framework backend for tatara guests.

The **bare-metal** VM engine. Direct `hv_vm_*` / `hv_vcpu_*` calls
via the `applevisor` safe-wrapper crate, own virtio device backends
(landing H.2.2), raw vCPU loop with MMIO callbacks.

[§](https://docs.rs#layering)Layering

```
  tatara-hvf (this crate)
      │  uses
      ▼
  applevisor (safe wrapper — Quarkslab)
      │  links
      ▼
  Hypervisor.framework  (aarch64-darwin only)
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cargo--build)Cargo / build

The `applevisor` dep is target-gated to `aarch64-darwin`. On any
other target, the crate compiles but `HvfEngine::new()` returns
`HvfError::UnsupportedPlatform`. This keeps `cargo check --workspace` clean on Linux CI while the real engine is only
exercised on M-series Macs.

[§](https://docs.rs#entitlements)Entitlements

Running any HVF binary requires the `com.apple.security.hypervisor`
entitlement. For `cargo test`, either codesign the test binary
with an entitlements plist or run tests as root. Currently:

```
codesign --entitlements entitlements.plist --sign - \
  target/debug/deps/tatara_hvf-*
```
A follow-up CI helper crate will encapsulate this; for now the
`vm_create_is_supported` test is `#[ignore]` by default so `cargo test` doesn’t fail when entitlements aren’t set.

# tatara_build_remote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-build-remote/0.2.122/tatara_build_remote/

## Expand description

`tatara-build-remote` — layered Nix build transport for tatara guests.

Takes a `BuildRef` (flake + attr, raw Nix expression, store path, or
OCI image) and resolves it to a concrete `StorePath` using a
priority-ordered chain of transports. **First match wins.** Default
chain:

- **Attic cache**— pulls from a shared Attic instance (e.g.- `quero.lol`). Fastest path when the artifact is already cached.
- **ssh-ng remote builder**— submits to a remote Nix builder over- `ssh-ng://`. Used when Attic misses and the local machine can’t or shouldn’t build (cross-arch, resource constrained, etc.).
- **Local**—- `nix build`on the host. Last resort.

Any transport declared absent in the spec is skipped. If all declared
transports fail, `BuildError::AllTransportsFailed` bubbles up and
hospedeiro refuses to boot the guest — we fail closed.

[§](https://docs.rs#status)Status

**Phase H.5 landed.** `AtticTransport`, `SshRemoteTransport`, and
`LocalTransport` all ship in `transports.rs`.
`BuildTransportChain::to_layered()` composes them into a priority-
ordered `LayeredTransport` driven by `(defguest …)`’s `:build-on`
keyword.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-layered-not-single-target)Why layered, not single-target

The fleet at `quero.lol` has a shared Attic cache *and* an ssh-ng
builder pool. Cache hits are free; builds are expensive. Layering
lets the common case (pleme-io team members pulling pre-built
artifacts) skip the slow path entirely. Keys + SSH config come from
the cid node’s `pangea-builder.nix` — no new auth plumbing.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use transports::`- [AtticTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.AtticTransport.html);
- `pub use transports::`- [LocalTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.LocalTransport.html);
- `pub use transports::`- [SshRemoteTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.SshRemoteTransport.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [transports](https://docs.rs/transports/index.html)
- Concrete `BuildTransport`implementations.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Build](https://docs.rs/struct.BuildTransportChain.html)- Transport - Chain
- Declarative transport chain. A `None`field means “don’t try this transport”.
- [Layered](https://docs.rs/struct.LayeredTransport.html)- Transport
- Layered transport — tries each child in order, returns the first success.
- [Store](https://docs.rs/struct.StorePath.html)- Path
- A Nix store path — content-addressed handle.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Build](https://docs.rs/enum.BuildError.html)- Error
- [Build](https://docs.rs/enum.BuildRef.html)- Ref
- A reference to something that becomes a Nix store path.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [CRATE_](https://docs.rs/constant.CRATE_STATUS.html)- STATUS
- Phase marker. Bumped by each phase that lands a change.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- The operation-level transport trait. Phase H.5 implements
`AtticTransport`,`SshRemoteTransport`, and`LocalTransport`.

# tatara_lisp_derive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-lisp-derive/0.2.122/tatara_lisp_derive/

## Expand description

`#[derive(TataraDomain)]` — generate a `TataraDomain` impl from a Rust struct.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use tatara_lisp_derive::TataraDomain;
#[derive(TataraDomain)]
#[tatara(keyword = "defmonitor")]
pub struct MonitorSpec {
    pub name: String,
    pub query: String,
    pub threshold: f64,
    pub window_seconds: Option<i64>,
}
```
Generates:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl TataraDomain for MonitorSpec {
    const KEYWORD: &'static str = "defmonitor";
    fn compile_from_args(args: &[Sexp]) -> Result<Self> {
        let kw = parse_kwargs_strict(args, __TATARA_ALLOWED_KEYWORDS)?;
        Ok(Self {
            name: extract_string(&kw, "name")?.to_string(),
            query: extract_string(&kw, "query")?.to_string(),
            threshold: extract_float(&kw, "threshold")?,
            window_seconds: extract_optional_int(&kw, "window-seconds")?,
        })
    }
}
```
Invoked from Lisp:

`(defmonitor :name "prom-up" :query "up{…}" :threshold 0.99 :window-seconds 300)`Supported field types (v0):

- `String`,- `Option<String>`,- `Vec<String>`
- `i64`,- `i32`,- `u32`,- `usize`,- `u64`,- `Option<i64>`
- `f64`,- `f32`,- `Option<f64>`
- `bool`,- `Option<bool>`

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Closed](https://docs.rs/derive.ClosedSet.html)- Set
- `#[derive(ClosedSet)]`— emit the substrate-wide [- `tatara_lisp::ClosedSet`] impl + the matching- `std::str::FromStr`- `ALL`+ projection +- `Unknown`+- `FromStr`shape).

# diffler - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/diffler/0.2.7/diffler/

## Expand description

diffler binary internals, exposed as a library so the integration tests can drive the full app (event pump + MCP server) headlessly. The public surface is the binary’s: nothing here is a stable API.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [app](https://docs.rs/app/index.html)
- Application state and event handling. `App::handle`is a pure-ish state transition (no terminal IO) so the whole shell is unit-testable; rendering reads the state in`ui::draw`. Per-screen state and handlers live in the`status`,`log`, and`diff`submodules.
- [ci](https://docs.rs/ci/index.html)
- Provider-agnostic CI run/job/log acquisition, plus the host glue that picks a
provider for the repo and maps a normalized `RunDetail`onto the graph model. Adapters (`providers/`) implement`CiProvider``gh`/`glab`/`curl`through the`CommandRunner`
- [clipboard](https://docs.rs/clipboard/index.html)
- System clipboard. Two mechanisms, used together for reach without native build deps (so the static musl binaries stay clean): an OSC52 escape sequence — written to the terminal by the main loop after a draw, never from rendering — which the terminal forwards even over ssh/tmux; and a best-effort pipe to the platform clipboard CLI, covering terminals that don’t honor OSC52.
- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- Layered TOML configuration: defaults → global file → project file → CLI.
- [editor](https://docs.rs/editor/index.html)
- $EDITOR integration. The TUI loop owns the terminal, so opening an
editor is a request: `App`queues an`EditorRequest``App::editor_finished`.
- [event](https://docs.rs/event/index.html)
- Terminal event pump: crossterm’s async stream plus a periodic tick,
multiplexed onto one channel. Kept thin — all decisions live in
`App::handle`, which is what the tests drive.
- [graph](https://docs.rs/graph/index.html)
- A navigable orthogonal node-graph component for ratatui, plus the host glue
mapping the app theme onto its palette. The component is IO-free (no terminal
setup, event loop, or network); the host builds a `Model``GraphView``GraphAction`
- [keymap](https://docs.rs/keymap/index.html)
- Key bindings: neogit-style defaults per screen, overridable from
`[keys.*]`config sections, with multi-key sequence resolution.
- [mcp](https://docs.rs/mcp/index.html)
- Embedded MCP server: agents read review comments, answer them in place,
and long-poll for the human’s feedback. Tool handlers never touch the
review directly — every call is sent through the app event channel as an
`McpRequest``App::handle_mcp`on the main loop, so the app stays the single owner of all state (no locks).
- [search](https://docs.rs/search/index.html)
- Vim-style `/`search. A pane feeds`Search``(row index, text)`; the search holds the query, matches, and active match, and drives incremental highlight +`n`/`N`navigation. Matching is plain substring with smartcase: case-insensitive unless the query has an uppercase letter.
- [theme](https://docs.rs/theme/index.html)
- Color themes. `github-dark`is the default;`ui.theme`selects a built-in, each pairing its palette with a matching syntax-highlight theme.
- [transient](https://docs.rs/transient/index.html)
- Magit/neogit-style transient menus: a top-level prefix key opens a transient whose own keys are pure leaves (immediate actions). The model is data, not closures, so resolution and the which-key panel layout stay pure and unit-testable; the app owns the live transient state and timer.
- [tree](https://docs.rs/tree/index.html)
- Pure directory-trie flattening shared by the diff sidebar and the status sections. A file list (repo-relative paths, in input order) becomes a list of visible rows honoring fold state — directories before files at each level, input order preserved within a kind, folded directories hiding their subtree. No rendering and no app state, so the navigation math is fully unit-testable.
- [ui](https://docs.rs/ui/index.html)
- Rendering. `draw`never computes review state; it reads`App`(the diff view additionally fills its lazy highlight cache and follows the cursor with its scroll offset, which is why it takes`&mut App`).
- [watch](https://docs.rs/watch/index.html)
- Filesystem watcher: debounced notify events on the repo become
`AppEvent::RepoChanged`. Noise sources (the session store, lockfiles, git’s object database) are filtered out so staging or saving a comment does not echo back as a repo change.

# surtgis_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/surtgis-core/0.17.0/surtgis_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#surtgis-core)SurtGis Core

Core types, traits and I/O for the SurtGis geospatial library.

This crate provides:

- `Raster<T>`: Generic raster grid type
- `GeoTransform`: Affine transformation for georeferencing
- `CRS`: Coordinate Reference System handling
- Algorithm traits for consistent API
- I/O for common geospatial formats
- Streaming (`StripProcessor``TileGrid`

[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

As of v0.15.0, `surtgis-core` is the foundation of the SurtGIS
engine ecosystem and its public API is treated as **stable under
SemVer**: within a minor series the API only grows, and breaking
changes are pre-announced one release ahead in the CHANGELOG under
a `Breaking` heading. Sibling crates should depend on
`surtgis-core = "0.15"` alone; the CLI and GUI crates carry no
stability promise.

The projections: from a `ResolvedModel` to Postgres DDL and an agnostic UI contract (JSON).

eval’d string, and they are the SAME domains the server compiles to SQL.

# 🦀 crabenv

The simplest, opinionated way to keep .env files, schemas, and examples aligned.

`crabenv` is an env var management standard created by [Carlo Taleon](http://carlo.tl) to minimize env var schema + documentation drift in any codebase. If you follow this standard, you'll find it extremely seamless to "develop locally" and "deploy to production" in any platform!

## Why use it

- Typesafety & Validation
- Good documentation. Never stale, does what it says.
-  Seamless *local development*to*deployment*story.
- No new config files. Your team doesn't need to install crabenv, it's just manual-crud made automated via CLI.
- Language-agnostic. No need to learn language-specific configurations for multi-language and monorepos, just use the same CLI commands.

- A senior dev wants to deploy a monorepo so what env vars needed for specific apps? Show them all with `crabenv ls`

- A senior dev wants to check for any drift? `crabenv doctor`

# shikumi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/shikumi/0.1.122/shikumi/

## Expand description

Shikumi (仕組み) — config discovery, hot-reload, and `ArcSwap` store
for Nix-managed desktop applications.

Extracted from [karakuri](https://github.com/pleme-io/karakuri)’s configuration
system, shikumi provides the shared infrastructure for desktop apps that need:

- **XDG config discovery**with env var overrides and format preference
- **Figment provider chains**(defaults → env vars → config file)
- **Lock-free concurrent reads**via- `ArcSwap`
- **Hot-reload**with symlink-aware file watching (for nix-darwin managed configs)

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use serde::Deserialize;
use shikumi::{ConfigDiscovery, ConfigStore, Format};
#[derive(Deserialize, Clone, Debug, Default)]
struct MyConfig {
    window_width: Option<u32>,
}
let path = ConfigDiscovery::new("myapp")
    .env_override("MYAPP_CONFIG")
    .formats(&[Format::Yaml, Format::Toml])
    .discover()
    .expect("config file not found");
let store = ConfigStore::<MyConfig>::load(&path, "MYAPP_")
    .expect("failed to load config");
let config = store.get();
println!("width: {:?}", config.window_width);
```

# camino 1.2.4 - Docs.rs

# camino - UTF-8 paths

This repository contains the source code for `camino`, an extension of the `std::path` module that adds new
[ Utf8PathBuf](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html) and

[types.](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`## What is camino?

`camino`'s [ Utf8PathBuf](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html) and

[types are like the standard library's](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)

`PathBuf`[types, except they are guaranteed to only contain UTF-8 encoded data. Therefore, they expose the ability to get their contents as strings, they implement](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path``Display`, etc.The `std::path` types are not guaranteed to be valid UTF-8. This is the right decision for the standard library,
since it must be as general as possible. However, on all platforms, non-Unicode paths are vanishingly uncommon for a
number of reasons:

- Unicode is now the dominant encoding for file names. There are still some legacy codebases that store paths in encodings like [Shift JIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shift_JIS), but most have been converted to Unicode at this point.
- Unicode is the common subset of supported paths across Windows and Unix platforms. (On Windows, Rust stores paths
as [an extension to UTF-8](https://simonsapin.github.io/wtf-8/), and converts them to UTF-16 at Win32 API boundaries.)
- There are already many systems, such as Cargo, that only support UTF-8 paths. If your own tool interacts with any such system, you can assume that paths are valid UTF-8 without creating any additional burdens on consumers.
- The ["makefile problem"](https://www.mercurial-scm.org/wiki/EncodingStrategy#The_.22makefile_problem.22)asks: given a Makefile or other metadata file (such as`Cargo.toml`) that lists the names of other files, how should the names in the Makefile be matched with the ones on disk? This has*no general, cross-platform solution*in systems that support non-UTF-8 paths. However, restricting paths to UTF-8 eliminates this problem.

Therefore, many programs that want to manipulate paths *do* assume they contain UTF-8 data, and convert them to `str`s
as necessary. However, because this invariant is not encoded in the `Path` type, conversions such as
`path.to_str().unwrap()` need to be repeated again and again, creating a frustrating experience.

Instead, `camino` allows you to check that your paths are UTF-8 *once*, and then manipulate them
as valid UTF-8 from there on, avoiding repeated lossy and confusing conversions.

## Examples

The documentation for [ Utf8PathBuf](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html) and

[contains several examples.](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`For examples of how to use `camino` with other libraries like `serde` and `clap`, see the [ camino-examples](https://github.com/camino-rs/camino/tree/main/camino-examples) directory.

## API design

`camino` is a very thin wrapper around `std::path`. [ Utf8Path](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html) and

[are drop-in replacements for](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html)

`Utf8PathBuf`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)

`PathBuf`Most APIs are the same, but those at the boundary with `str` are different. Some examples:

- `Path::to_str() -> Option<&str>`has been renamed to- `Utf8Path::as_str() -> &str`.
- `Utf8Path`- `Display`, and- `Path::display()`has been removed.
- Iterating over a `Utf8Path``&str`, not`&OsStr`.

Every [ Utf8Path](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html) is a valid

[, so](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[implements](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path``AsRef<Path>`. Any APIs that accept `impl AsRef<Path>`
will continue to work with [instances.](https://docs.rs/camino/*/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`## Should you use camino?

`camino` trades off some utility for a great deal of simplicity. Whether `camino` is appropriate for a project or not
is ultimately a case-by-case decision. Here are some general guidelines that may help.

*You should consider using camino if...*

- **You're building portable, cross-platform software.**While both Unix and Windows platforms support different kinds of non-Unicode paths, Unicode is the common subset that's supported across them.
- **Your system has files that contain the names of other files.**If you don't use UTF-8 paths, you will run into the makefile problem described above, which has no general, cross-platform solution.
- **You're interacting with existing systems that already assume UTF-8 paths.**In that case you won't be adding any new burdens on downstream consumers.
- **You're building something brand new and are willing to ask your users to rename their paths if necessary.**Projects that don't have to worry about legacy compatibility have more flexibility in choosing what paths they support.

In general, using camino is the right choice for most projects.

*You should  NOT use camino, if...*

- **You're writing a core system utility.**If you're writing, say, an- `mv`or- `cat`replacement, you should- **not**use camino. Instead, use- `std::path::Path`
- **You have legacy compatibility constraints.**For example, Git supports non-UTF-8 paths. If your tool needs to handle arbitrary Git repositories, it should use its own path type that's a wrapper around- `Vec<u8>`.- `std::path::Path`- [on Unix](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/ffi/index.html)but not on Windows.

- **There's some other reason you need to support non-UTF-8 paths.**Some tools like disk recovery utilities need to handle potentially corrupt filenames: only being able to handle UTF-8 paths would greatly diminish their utility.

## Optional features

By default, `camino` has **no dependencies** other than `std`. There are some optional features that enable
dependencies:

- `serde1`adds serde- `Serialize`- `Deserialize`- `Utf8PathBuf`- `Utf8Path`
- `proptest1`adds- [proptest](https://altsysrq.github.io/proptest-book/)- `Arbitrary`- `Utf8PathBuf`- `Box<Utf8Path>`.

## Rust version support

The minimum supported Rust version (MSRV) for `camino` with default features is **1.61**. This project is tested in CI
against the latest stable version of Rust and the MSRV.

- *Stable APIs*added in later Rust versions are supported either through conditional compilation in- `build.rs`, or through backfills that also work on older versions.
- *Deprecations*are kept in sync with the version of Rust they're added in.
- *Unstable APIs*are currently not supported. Please- [file an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/camino-rs/camino/issues/new)if you need an unstable API.

`camino` is designed to be a core library and has a conservative MSRV policy. MSRV increases will only happen for
a compelling enough reason, and will involve at least a minor version bump.

Optional features may pull in dependencies that require a newer version of Rust.

## License

This project is available under the terms of either the [Apache 2.0 license](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) or the [MIT
license](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT).

This project's documentation is adapted from [The Rust Programming Language](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/), which is
available under the terms of either the [Apache 2.0 license](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/LICENSE-APACHE)
or the [MIT license](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/LICENSE-MIT).

- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8Path.html)- Path
- A slice of a UTF-8 path (akin to `str`
- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html)- Path - Buf
- An owned, mutable UTF-8 path (akin to `String`
- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8PrefixComponent.html)- Prefix - Component
- A structure wrapping a Windows path prefix as well as its unparsed string representation.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/enum.Utf8Component.html)- Component
- A single component of a path.
- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/enum.Utf8Prefix.html)- Prefix
- Windows path prefixes, e.g., `C:`or`\\server\share`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [absolute_](https://docs.rs/fn.absolute_utf8.html)- utf8 - `absolute_path`
- Makes the path absolute without accessing the filesystem, converting it to a `Utf8PathBuf`

# camino/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)// Copyright (c) The camino Contributors
[2](https://docs.rs#2)// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0
[3](https://docs.rs#3)
[4](https://docs.rs#4)#![warn(missing_docs)]
[5](https://docs.rs#5)#![cfg_attr(doc_cfg, feature(doc_cfg))]
[6](https://docs.rs#6)
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! UTF-8 encoded paths.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! `camino` is an extension of the [`std::path`] module that adds new [`Utf8PathBuf`] and [`Utf8Path`]
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! types. These are like the standard library's [`PathBuf`] and [`Path`] types, except they are
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! guaranteed to only contain UTF-8 encoded data. Therefore, they expose the ability to get their
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! contents as strings, they implement [`Display`], etc.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! The [`std::path`] types are not guaranteed to be valid UTF-8. This is the right decision for the standard library,
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! since it must be as general as possible. However, on all platforms, non-Unicode paths are vanishingly uncommon for a
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! number of reasons:
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! * Unicode won. There are still some legacy codebases that store paths in encodings like Shift-JIS, but most
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!   have been converted to Unicode at this point.
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! * Unicode is the common subset of supported paths across Windows and Unix platforms. (On Windows, Rust stores paths
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!   as [an extension to UTF-8](https://simonsapin.github.io/wtf-8/), and converts them to UTF-16 at Win32
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!   API boundaries.)
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! * There are already many systems, such as Cargo, that only support UTF-8 paths. If your own tool interacts with any such
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!   system, you can assume that paths are valid UTF-8 without creating any additional burdens on consumers.
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! * The ["makefile problem"](https://www.mercurial-scm.org/wiki/EncodingStrategy#The_.22makefile_problem.22)
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!   (which also applies to `Cargo.toml`, and any other metadata file that lists the names of other files) has *no general,
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!   cross-platform solution* in systems that support non-UTF-8 paths. However, restricting paths to UTF-8 eliminates
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!   this problem.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! Therefore, many programs that want to manipulate paths *do* assume they contain UTF-8 data, and convert them to [`str`]s
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! as  necessary. However, because this invariant is not encoded in the [`Path`] type, conversions such as
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! `path.to_str().unwrap()` need to be repeated again and again, creating a frustrating experience.
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! Instead, `camino` allows you to check that your paths are UTF-8 *once*, and then manipulate them
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! as valid UTF-8 from there on, avoiding repeated lossy and confusing conversions.
[35](https://docs.rs#35)
[36](https://docs.rs#36)// General note: we use #[allow(clippy::incompatible_msrv)] for code that's already guarded by a
[37](https://docs.rs#37)// version-specific cfg conditional.
[38](https://docs.rs#38)

[45](https://docs.rs#45)    fmt,

[64](https://docs.rs#64)/// An owned, mutable UTF-8 path (akin to [`String`]).
[65](https://docs.rs#65)///
[66](https://docs.rs#66)/// This type provides methods like [`push`] and [`set_extension`] that mutate
[67](https://docs.rs#67)/// the path in place. It also implements [`Deref`] to [`Utf8Path`], meaning that
[68](https://docs.rs#68)/// all methods on [`Utf8Path`] slices are available on [`Utf8PathBuf`] values as well.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)///
[70](https://docs.rs#70)/// [`push`]: Utf8PathBuf::push
[71](https://docs.rs#71)/// [`set_extension`]: Utf8PathBuf::set_extension
[72](https://docs.rs#72)///
[73](https://docs.rs#73)/// # Examples
[74](https://docs.rs#74)///
[75](https://docs.rs#75)/// You can use [`push`] to build up a [`Utf8PathBuf`] from
[76](https://docs.rs#76)/// components:
[77](https://docs.rs#77)///
[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// ```
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// use camino::Utf8PathBuf;
[80](https://docs.rs#80)///
[81](https://docs.rs#81)/// let mut path = Utf8PathBuf::new();
[82](https://docs.rs#82)///
[83](https://docs.rs#83)/// path.push(r"C:\");
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// path.push("windows");
[85](https://docs.rs#85)/// path.push("system32");
[86](https://docs.rs#86)///
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// path.set_extension("dll");
[88](https://docs.rs#88)/// ```
[89](https://docs.rs#89)///
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// However, [`push`] is best used for dynamic situations. This is a better way
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// to do this when you know all of the components ahead of time:
[92](https://docs.rs#92)///
[93](https://docs.rs#93)/// ```
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// use camino::Utf8PathBuf;
[95](https://docs.rs#95)///
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// let path: Utf8PathBuf = [r"C:\", "windows", "system32.dll"].iter().collect();
[97](https://docs.rs#97)/// ```
[98](https://docs.rs#98)///
[99](https://docs.rs#99)/// We can still do better than this! Since these are all strings, we can use
[100](https://docs.rs#100)/// [`From::from`]:
[101](https://docs.rs#101)///
[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// ```
[103](https://docs.rs#103)/// use camino::Utf8PathBuf;
[104](https://docs.rs#104)///
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// let path = Utf8PathBuf::from(r"C:\windows\system32.dll");
[106](https://docs.rs#106)/// ```
[107](https://docs.rs#107)///
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// Which method works best depends on what kind of situation you're in.
[109](https://docs.rs#109)// NB: Internal PathBuf must only contain utf8 data
[110](https://docs.rs#110)#[derive(Clone, Default)]
[111](https://docs.rs#111)#[repr(transparent)]
[112](https://docs.rs#112)pub struct Utf8PathBuf(PathBuf);
[113](https://docs.rs#113)

[288](https://docs.rs#288)    /// Consumes and leaks the [`Utf8PathBuf`], returning a mutable reference to the contents,
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    /// `&'a mut Utf8Path`.
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    ///
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    /// The caller has free choice over the returned lifetime, including 'static.
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    /// Indeed, this function is ideally used for data that lives for the remainder of
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    /// the program’s life, as dropping the returned reference will cause a memory leak.
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    ///
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    /// It does not reallocate or shrink the [`Utf8PathBuf`], so the leaked allocation may include
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    /// unused capacity that is not part of the returned slice. If you want to discard excess
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    /// capacity, call [`into_boxed_path`], and then [`Box::leak`] instead.
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    /// However, keep in mind that trimming the capacity may result in a reallocation and copy.
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    ///
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    /// *Requires Rust 1.89 or newer.*
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    ///
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    /// [`into_boxed_path`]: Self::into_boxed_path
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    #[cfg(os_string_pathbuf_leak)]
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    #[allow(clippy::incompatible_msrv)]
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    #[inline]
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    pub fn leak<'a>(self) -> &'a mut Utf8Path {
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        // SAFETY: every Utf8PathBuf constructor ensures that self is valid UTF-8
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        unsafe { Utf8Path::assume_utf8_mut(self.0.leak()) }
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    }

[311](https://docs.rs#311)    /// Extends `self` with `path`.
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    ///
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    /// If `path` is absolute, it replaces the current path.
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    ///
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// On Windows:
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    ///
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    /// * if `path` has a root but no prefix (e.g., `\windows`), it
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    ///   replaces everything except for the prefix (if any) of `self`.
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    /// * if `path` has a prefix but no root, it replaces `self`.
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    ///
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    /// # Examples
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    ///
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    /// Pushing a relative path extends the existing path:
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    ///
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    /// ```
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    /// use camino::Utf8PathBuf;
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    ///
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    /// let mut path = Utf8PathBuf::from("/tmp");
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    /// path.push("file.bk");
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    /// assert_eq!(path, Utf8PathBuf::from("/tmp/file.bk"));
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    /// ```
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    ///
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    /// Pushing an absolute path replaces the existing path:
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    ///
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    /// ```
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    /// use camino::Utf8PathBuf;
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    ///
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    /// let mut path = Utf8PathBuf::from("/tmp");
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    /// path.push("/etc");
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    /// assert_eq!(path, Utf8PathBuf::from("/etc"));
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// ```
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    pub fn push(&mut self, path: impl AsRef<Utf8Path>) {
[343](https://docs.rs#343)        self.0.push(&path.as_ref().0)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    }
[345](https://docs.rs#345)
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    /// Truncates `self` to [`self.parent`].
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    ///
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    /// Returns `false` and does nothing if [`self.parent`] is [`None`].
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    /// Otherwise, returns `true`.
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    ///
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    /// [`self.parent`]: Utf8Path::parent
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    ///
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    /// # Examples
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    ///
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    /// ```
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    /// use camino::{Utf8Path, Utf8PathBuf};
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    ///
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    /// let mut p = Utf8PathBuf::from("/spirited/away.rs");
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    ///
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// p.pop();

[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// ```

[366](https://docs.rs#366)        self.0.pop()
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    }
[368](https://docs.rs#368)
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// Updates [`self.file_name`] to `file_name`.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    ///
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// If [`self.file_name`] was [`None`], this is equivalent to pushing
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// `file_name`.
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    ///
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    /// Otherwise it is equivalent to calling [`pop`] and then pushing
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    /// `file_name`. The new path will be a sibling of the original path.
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    /// (That is, it will have the same parent.)
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    ///
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /// [`self.file_name`]: Utf8Path::file_name
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    /// [`pop`]: Utf8PathBuf::pop
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    ///
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// # Examples
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    ///
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    /// ```
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// use camino::Utf8PathBuf;
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    ///
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    /// let mut buf = Utf8PathBuf::from("/");
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// assert_eq!(buf.file_name(), None);
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    /// buf.set_file_name("bar");
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    /// assert_eq!(buf, Utf8PathBuf::from("/bar"));
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    /// assert!(buf.file_name().is_some());
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    /// buf.set_file_name("baz.txt");
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// assert_eq!(buf, Utf8PathBuf::from("/baz.txt"));
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// ```
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    pub fn set_file_name(&mut self, file_name: impl AsRef<str>) {
[395](https://docs.rs#395)        self.0.set_file_name(file_name.as_ref())
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    }

[398](https://docs.rs#398)    /// Updates [`self.extension`] to `extension`.

[413](https://docs.rs#413)    ///
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    /// let mut p = Utf8PathBuf::from("/feel/the");
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    ///

[424](https://docs.rs#424)    }

[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// Appends to [`self.extension`] with `extension`.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    ///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// Returns `false` and does nothing if [`self.file_name`] is [`None`],
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// returns `true` and updates the extension otherwise.
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    ///
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    /// *Requires Rust 1.91 or newer.*
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    ///
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    /// # Panics
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    ///
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// Panics if the passed extension contains a path separator (see
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// [`is_separator`]).
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    ///
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// # Caveats
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    ///
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// The appended `extension` may contain dots and will be used in its entirety,
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    /// but only the part after the final dot will be reflected in [`self.extension`].
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    ///
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    /// [`self.file_name`]: Utf8Path::file_name
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    /// [`self.extension`]: Utf8Path::extension
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    ///
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    /// # Examples
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    ///
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    /// ```
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    /// use camino::{Utf8Path, Utf8PathBuf};
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    ///
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// let mut p = Utf8PathBuf::from("/feel/the");
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    ///
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    /// p.add_extension("formatted");
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// assert_eq!(Utf8Path::new("/feel/the.formatted"), p.as_path());
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    ///
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    /// p.add_extension("dark.side");
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    /// assert_eq!(Utf8Path::new("/feel/the.formatted.dark.side"), p.as_path());
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    /// ```
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    #[cfg(path_add_extension)]
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    #[expect(clippy::incompatible_msrv)]
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    pub fn add_extension<S: AsRef<str>>(&mut self, extension: S) -> bool {
[462](https://docs.rs#462)        self.0.add_extension(extension.as_ref())
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    }

[498](https://docs.rs#498)    /// Converts this [`Utf8PathBuf`] into a [boxed](Box) [`Utf8Path`].
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    #[must_use = "`self` will be dropped if the result is not used"]
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    pub fn into_boxed_path(self) -> Box<Utf8Path> {
[501](https://docs.rs#501)        let ptr = Box::into_raw(self.0.into_boxed_path()) as *mut Utf8Path;
[502](https://docs.rs#502)        // SAFETY:
[503](https://docs.rs#503)        // * self is valid UTF-8
[504](https://docs.rs#504)        // * ptr was constructed by consuming self so it represents an owned path
[505](https://docs.rs#505)        // * Utf8Path is marked as #[repr(transparent)] so the conversion from *mut Path to
[506](https://docs.rs#506)        //   *mut Utf8Path is valid
[507](https://docs.rs#507)        unsafe { Box::from_raw(ptr) }
[508](https://docs.rs#508)    }
